title: The Golden Room and the Center of the World: Bucharest, Calcutta, Lisbon, Ascona, Chicago
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Bucharest, the birth and the two dates
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Romanian Wikipedia gives the archival date plainly, 28 February / 13 March 1907, Old Style and New. Eliade's own Autobiography opens 'M-am nascut la Bucuresti, la 9 martie 1907 (25 februarie stil vechi)', a self-dating four days off the registry that he repeated all his life, so the discrepancy is his rather than the sources'. The birth address is not established: the family bought the Melodiei house only in 1914, so the pin is the quarter and not the room.
stops.campa: A son is born to Gheorghe Eliade, an infantry officer who has changed the family name from Ieremia, and to Jeana Vasilescu, in a Bucharest of garrison postings and Orthodox feast days. The registry keeps the thirteenth of March. The son will keep the ninth all his life, Old Style the twenty-fifth of February, and will open his autobiography with it. The father is said to have moved the date to reach the feast of the Forty Martyrs. Nobody corrects him, and the registry entry is never amended.
suggested_refs: The Bucharest civil register entry of 1907 against the opening page of Eliade's Autobiography, Volume I

stops.name: Tecuci, the garrison postings
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The English Wikipedia account places a Moldavian garrison posting at Tecuci among the family's moves before they settle in Bucharest in 1914; no month is given, and the year here is inferred backward from that settlement date.
stops.campa: The army moves the family from posting to posting through Moldavia, and Tecuci holds them for a season: a small town on the Barlad, its garrison, its dust, its weekly market. The boy is six. He collects insects, keeps notebooks on them, and reads anything left on a shelf. The memoirs barely reopen Tecuci later, though nearly every other room of his childhood is eventually produced as evidence. The family reaches Bucharest in 1914 and does not move again.
suggested_refs: The Romanian army garrison registers for Tecuci, 1912-1914

stops.name: Melodiei Street, the room full of gold
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the house: Romanian Wikipedia records the 1914 purchase of a house at 1 Strada Melodiei, now Strada Radu Cristian, where Eliade lived into late adolescence. The golden-room episode is Eliade's own memoir testimony and is corroborated by no third party; no source consulted places it in this particular house, so the localization is inference. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: The Eliades buy a house at 1 Melodiei Street, near Piata Rosetti, and the boy is given the run of it. In one drawing room, entered by accident at an hour when the light comes through green glass, he finds the whole space filled with a gold he can taste. He tells no one at the time. He teaches himself instead to summon that minute back on command, lying still and waiting for it, and he keeps the exercise up for years. It is the first hierophany in a life spent naming them, and it happens before he has any word for it.
stops.quote: I practiced for many years this exercise of recapturing the epiphanic moment, and I would always find again the same plenitude.
stops.quote_source: Mircea Eliade, Autobiography, Volume I: Journey East, Journey West, 1907-1937
suggested_refs: The house at 1 Strada Melodiei, now Strada Radu Cristian, Bucharest
Saul Bellow's reading of this passage at the memorial service, Chicago, 1986
sources: Mircea Eliade, Autobiography, Volume I, verified by full-text search at Open Library
Robert Ellwood, The Politics of Myth

stops.name: Mantuleasa Street, the primary school
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade attended primary school on Mantuleasa Street, per the English Wikipedia article; the month is a default for the start of a school year. The coordinate is Nominatim's for Strada Mantuleasa and corrects an earlier working figure that sat 800 metres southwest of the street it named.
stops.campa: He walks to primary school on Strada Mantuleasa, a street of low houses, walled gardens and one old church in the Armenian quarter of Bucharest. Fifty-three years later he writes a novella called Pe strada Mantuleasa, in which a retired schoolmaster is interrogated by the secret police and answers only in stories that refuse to end, until the interrogation has become the folk tale and the interrogators are inside it. The schoolmaster is invented. The street is not, and neither is the church at number 20, brick, behind its wall.
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Pe strada Mantuleasa (1967), translated as The Old Man and the Bureaucrats

stops.name: Spiru Haret College, the enemy of the silkworm
stops.date_confidence: Attested: secondary schooling at the Spiru Haret National College and a first published article in 1921 on the enemy of the silkworm, both per the English Wikipedia article; no month is given. The coordinate is Nominatim's for Colegiul National Spiru Haret on Strada Otetari and corrects an earlier working figure off by about 1.1 kilometres.
stops.campa: At the Spiru Haret National College he is a bad sleeper by design, cutting his nights to four hours to buy reading time and ruining eyes already weak. He keeps insects in jars, runs chemistry in an attic room, and in 1921 places his first article in a popular-science weekly: the enemy of the silkworm. He is fourteen. Before he leaves the school he has published dozens of pieces and drafted a novel about adolescence, and he has decided that the discipline of the naturalist and the discipline of the ascetic are one discipline.
suggested_refs: Eliade's adolescent popular-science journalism, 1921-1925, and the Romanul adolescentului miop
sources: Nominatim, Colegiul National Spiru Haret, Bucharest

stops.name: University of Bucharest, Nae Ionescu at the lectern
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the enrolment years 1925-1928 and for the diploma on Tommaso Campanella, per the English Wikipedia article; the month is a default. The wider Ficino-to-Bruno scope often given for the thesis is reconstruction: a term search of that article returns no occurrence of Ficino, and the scope would have to be cited to Ricketts or Turcanu directly.
stops.campa: He enrols in philosophy and letters and finds Nae Ionescu at the lectern: logician, newspaper editor, and the pole around which the whole young generation of Bucharest arranges itself. Ionescu teaches that thought has to be lived rather than systematized, and his students take him at his word in every available direction, some toward mysticism, some toward the Legion, some toward both at once. Eliade will call him his master for the rest of his life. The diploma he takes in 1928 is a study of Tommaso Campanella.
suggested_refs: Nae Ionescu's lecture courses at the University of Bucharest, 1925-1940
Eliade's diploma thesis on Tommaso Campanella

segments.name: Italy, the Suez Passage, and Calcutta

stops.name: Florence, at Papini's door
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade travelled to Italy in 1927 and met Giovanni Papini, per the English Wikipedia article; no month and no address are given, so the pin is the city centre and the month is a default. The claim, often repeated, that he also met Giuseppe Tucci in Italy on this trip is not supported by any source reached: that article says only that the two collaborated. The 1927 quotation is carried without an original periodical citation and is treated as reconstruction.
stops.campa: He goes to Italy on a student's budget, hunting manuscripts for the Renaissance thesis and hunting writers for himself, and gets as far as Giovanni Papini, the Florentine polemicist whose conversion narrative he has read the way other boys read adventure stories. The meeting is short and Papini is difficult. It does not much matter. Eliade is already publishing manifestos at home, telling the young men of Bucharest what a generation is for, and one of the things he tells them in 1927 is that what is wanted is the return to the Church.
stops.quote_source: Eliade's 1927 recommendation to young Romanian intellectuals, quoted on the English Wikipedia article 'Mircea Eliade' without an original periodical citation
suggested_refs: Giovanni Papini, Un uomo finito (1912), the book Eliade came to Florence carrying

stops.name: Port Said, the passage to India
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the port. The English Wikipedia article records only 'a brief visit to Egypt' before India and names no place; Port Said is the Suez-route call for a Calcutta-bound steamer and is used here as the inference. Alexandria, which some accounts supply, is not on that route. The stipend from the Maharaja of Kassimbazar and the autumn 1928 departure are attested. The day is a default.
stops.campa: A stipend from the Maharaja of Kassimbazar puts a twenty-one-year-old Romanian on a steamer for Calcutta, and the steamer goes through the canal. He stops in Egypt long enough for it to be recorded and not long enough for anyone to write down where. What survives is the shape of the passage: the Mediterranean, the cut through the desert, the Red Sea, then the long swing east into an ocean he has read about only in grammars. He is going out to learn Sanskrit from the man who wrote the history of Indian philosophy.
suggested_refs: The Suez transit registers for European steamers on the Calcutta run, autumn 1928

stops.name: Bhowanipore, in Dasgupta's house
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade lodged in Surendranath Dasgupta's household while studying under him, per the English Wikipedia article. The street address, 3 Bakul Bagan Road, occurs nowhere in that article and is carried from the dossier; Nominatim puts Bakul Bagan Road at 22.5277, 88.3502. The pin used here is the canonical corpus coordinate for the Dasgupta house, inherited from giuseppe_tucci.journey.json. The Tucci meeting of 1929 is attested by that file. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: Surendranath Dasgupta takes the Romanian into his own house in Bhowanipore, and for two years Eliade eats at his table, reads Sanskrit at his desk, and works through the Yoga-sutras with him line by line. In 1929 an Italian comes to the same door: Giuseppe Tucci, teaching at Calcutta University, already halfway to Tibet. Two Europeans who will spend their lives explaining Asia to Europe sit in one Bengali drawing room, both of them at the start of it. Dasgupta's daughter Maitreyi, sixteen and already a published poet, is in the house.
suggested_refs: Surendranath Dasgupta, A History of Indian Philosophy, the work Eliade came to Calcutta to study under

stops.name: Bhowanipore, put out of the house
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the relationship with Maitreyi Devi developed inside the household and that Eliade was expelled from it, per the English Wikipedia article; the day and month are defaults. What passed between them is disputed at the source and is not adjudicated here: Eliade's 1933 novel Maitreyi tells it as consummated, and Devi's Na Hanyate of 1974 denies that account.
stops.campa: Dasgupta learns of it and puts him out of the house. Eliade leaves Calcutta, and the whole Indian apprenticeship turns, in time, into two books by two hands. His is a novel published in Bucharest in 1933 under her name: a prize, a sensation, the best-selling thing he ever writes in Romanian. Hers comes forty-one years later, written after she finally learns what he had printed about her, and it says the Romanian lied. Both books are still in print. Both are novels. No third account of that household has been found.
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Maitreyi (1933), translated as Bengal Nights
Maitreyi Devi, Na Hanyate (1974), translated as It Does Not Die

stops.name: Rishikesh, the Himalayan ashram
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The English Wikipedia article says only that Eliade 'spent a short period at a Himalayan ashram' and contains no occurrence of Rishikesh or of Sivananda; the identification is dossier-derived. The name Ananda Kutir is anachronistic for 1930, belonging to a Divine Life Society ashram founded in 1936. Sources also disagree on duration, 'a short period' against the months the dossier claims. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: He goes north to where the Ganges comes out of the hills, to an ashram, and does what the books he has been reading describe: posture, breath, retention, the disciplines whose whole object is to stop the mind from moving. How long he stays is not settled by anything reachable. What he carries away is a claim other scholars of yoga cannot make, that he has sat in the position as well as read the manual, and every yoga book he publishes for the next forty years rests part of its authority on this stretch of river.
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Yoga: Essai sur les origines de la mystique indienne (1936)

stops.name: University of Bucharest, the doctorate on yoga
stops.date_confidence: Attested: return to Romania at the end of 1931, compulsory military service, and the doctorate awarded by the University of Bucharest in 1933 for a thesis on yoga, all per the English Wikipedia article; the day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: He comes home at the end of 1931, serves his compulsory year, and turns the Calcutta notebooks into a thesis: Yoga, the psychology of Indian meditation. The university gives him the doctorate in 1933. Recast in French it becomes Yoga: Essai sur les origines de la mystique indienne, the first of the books that will make his name in the West, and the last written by a man who had recently been in the room where the practice was actually done. He also starts lecturing, unpaid, as Nae Ionescu's assistant.
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Yoga. Psihologia meditatiei indiene (Bucharest doctoral thesis, 1933)

stops.name: Sala Dalles, the Criterion symposia
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade was a leading figure in Criterion and that its public symposia, on Lenin, Freud, Gandhi, Chaplin and Mussolini, were disrupted by far-right students, per the English Wikipedia article. The venue is reconstruction: that article contains no occurrence of Dalles. The coordinate is Nominatim's for the Sala Dalles on Bulevardul Nicolae Balcescu, correcting a working figure that placed it on Calea Victoriei. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: Criterion fills a Bucharest hall with paying audiences who come to hear five young men argue in public about Lenin, about Freud, about Gandhi and Chaplin and Mussolini, one subject a night, each speaker assigned a different side. Eliade is on the platform with Petru Comarnescu, Mihail Sebastian, Emil Cioran, Constantin Noica and Eugene Ionesco. It is the last time this generation stands in a room together on those terms. Legionary students start coming to shout Sebastian down for being a Jew, and the symposia stop.
suggested_refs: Cristina A. Bejan, Intellectuals and Fascism in Interwar Romania: The Criterion Association (2019)

stops.name: Dacia Boulevard 141, the productive years
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the address and the household: 'the three of them moved to an apartment at 141 Dacia Boulevard' (English Wikipedia). Nominatim resolves the renumbered address as 171, formerly 141, and the coordinate here follows it, correcting a working figure off by 1.1 kilometres. The 1934 marriage to Nina Mares is attested by Romanian Wikipedia. The day and month are defaults. The quotation carries no original periodical citation and is treated as reconstruction.
stops.campa: He marries Nina Mares in 1934, and the two of them, with her daughter Adalgiza, take an apartment at 141 Dacia Boulevard. Out of these rooms comes work at a rate that alarms his own friends: novels one after another, close to a thousand articles, running polemics with George Calinescu, a public quarrel a month. He is the most visible writer of his generation in Romania and he is twenty-seven. Accused of mystical excess, he answers that what he wants is total transformation and, for God's sake, in any direction but the spiritual.
stops.quote: All I wish for is a deep change, a complete transformation. But, for God's sake, in any direction other than spirituality.
stops.quote_source: Eliade, reply to George Calinescu's anti-modernist critique, summer 1933, quoted on the English Wikipedia article 'Mircea Eliade' without an original periodical citation
suggested_refs: The apartment at 171, formerly 141, Bulevardul Dacia, Bucharest

stops.name: Bucharest, the manifesto and the preface
stops.date_confidence: The 1933 half is attested verbatim: 'In 1933, he was among the signers of a manifesto opposing Nazi Germany's state-enforced racism' (English Wikipedia). The 1934 half corrects a common error carried in the working dossier: Eliade did not write the preface to Sebastian's De doua mii de ani. Nae Ionescu wrote it, on the eternal damnation of the Jews, and Eliade spoke publicly against that view. The day and month are defaults; the quoted phrase carries no original periodical citation.
stops.campa: In 1933 he signs a manifesto against Nazi racial law. The next year his friend Mihail Sebastian publishes a novel about being a Jew in Romania and asks his own teacher for a preface, and Nae Ionescu supplies one arguing that the Jews are damned eternally and cannot be saved. Sebastian prints it at the front of his book anyway. Eliade takes Sebastian's side in public, disputing his own master's theology in the press, and defines what he means by Romanianism: neither fascism, nor chauvinism.
stops.quote_source: Eliade's 1934 description of Romanianism, quoted on the English Wikipedia article 'Mircea Eliade' without an original periodical citation
suggested_refs: Mihail Sebastian, De doua mii de ani (1934), with Nae Ionescu's preface
Mihail Sebastian, Journal 1935-1944

stops.name: University of Bucharest, the assistant's course
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade served as Nae Ionescu's unpaid assistant at the University of Bucharest, lecturing on metaphysics and the history of religions. The English Wikipedia article dates the formal assistant-lecturer role narrowly to 1936-1937; other accounts run the association from 1933 to 1939. Both datings are recorded and neither is adjudicated here. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: He is given a course of his own, unpaid, under Ionescu's chair: metaphysics first, then the history of religions, then a seminar reading the Upanishads in Sanskrit. Students remember the lectures as performances, delivered without notes at speed, moving from Australian initiation rites to alchemy to the Bhagavad Gita inside a single hour. The method is already fixed here. Everything human is comparable to everything else human, and the comparison is itself the argument.
suggested_refs: Eliade's University of Bucharest lecture courses on metaphysics and the history of religions, 1933-1939

stops.name: Calea Victoriei, writing for Buna Vestire
stops.date_confidence: Attested that by 1937 Eliade publicly supported the Legionary Movement, enrolled in its electoral party and wrote for Buna Vestire and Sfarma-Piatra, per the English Wikipedia article. The quoted phrase is verified: The Oxford Handbook of Fascism quotes Eliade in Vremea, December 1936, on giving birth to a Christian revolution. The longer formulation often attributed to him, about a Christian revolution aimed at creating a new Romania, is a later writer's narration and not his published sentence. The pin is the Calea Victoriei press quarter, not a located office; the day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: He begins signing articles in the Legion's papers. The Iron Guard by now has a death cult, an assassination record and a leader, Corneliu Zelea Codreanu, who is worshipped rather than followed. Eliade writes that the movement's purpose is a Christian revolution, that it will reconcile Romania with God, that the nation is to be remade from the soul outward. Nobody is coercing him, and the articles carry his name. He is thirty, four years past the Criterion platform where he shared a stage with Sebastian.
stops.quote_source: Eliade in Vremea, December 1936, quoted in R. J. B. Bosworth, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Fascism
suggested_refs: Eliade's 1937 articles in Buna Vestire and Sfarma-Piatra
Z. Ornea, Anii treizeci: Extrema dreapta romaneasca
sources: R. J. B. Bosworth, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Fascism

stops.name: Prahova county, the December election
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the English Wikipedia article records Eliade's electoral campaign responsibilities in Prahova County for Totul pentru Tara in the December 1937 election. The pin is the county seat, Ploiesti, at Nominatim's coordinate, used as an approximation for a county-wide assignment; the day is a default. The quotation reaches here through a secondary chain, Wikipedia citing Ornea, and the underlying 1937 article was not consulted.
stops.campa: Totul pentru Tara, the Legion's electoral list, hands him Prahova: the oil fields, the refineries at Ploiesti, the towns strung up the valley toward the mountains. The Guard takes about sixteen percent nationally and becomes the third party in Romania. Within seven months the king has abolished the parties, Codreanu is in prison, and the men who campaigned for him are being collected one by one. Whether Eliade asked for the assignment or was handed it does not appear in any record consulted.
stops.quote_source: Eliade, 1937 article on the Legionary Movement, cited as Eliade 1937 in Z. Ornea, Anii treizeci: Extrema dreapta romaneasca, p. 203
suggested_refs: The December 1937 Romanian general election returns for Prahova County

stops.name: Bucharest, arrested at the Siguranta
stops.date_confidence: Attested: arrested 14 July 1938 in the crackdown on the Iron Guard under Carol II's royal dictatorship, and held about three weeks at Siguranta Statului headquarters, per the English Wikipedia article, which also states flatly that Eliade refused to sign the declaration of dissociation. The pin is central Bucharest; the headquarters address was not located in any source reached.
stops.campa: The king dissolves the parties, and the police start collecting everyone who wrote for the Guard. Eliade is taken on the fourteenth of July and held three weeks at the headquarters of the Siguranta. He is asked to sign a declaration dissociating himself from the Legionary Movement. He refuses. Both his defenders and his prosecutors have had to account for that refusal, and they read it in opposite directions. In early August he is put on a train for the mountains.
suggested_refs: The Siguranta Statului files on the July 1938 Legionary detentions

stops.name: Miercurea-Ciuc, the internment camp
stops.date_confidence: Attested: transfer to the Miercurea-Ciuc internment camp in early August 1938, per the English Wikipedia article; the day is a default. Nae Ionescu's presence in the same camp is frequently stated but is not in that article and is not attested by anything reached this pass. The coordinate is Nominatim's for Miercurea Ciuc.
stops.campa: They move him to a camp in the Szekler country, in the mountains at the far end of Transylvania, behind wire with several hundred other Legionary detainees. He reads, he keeps a notebook, he develops what the doctors call tuberculosis. That autumn Codreanu and thirteen others are taken out of a prison van on the road and strangled, the official account being that they were shot while attempting to escape. The camp hears of it. By then Eliade is coughing badly enough to be sent away.
suggested_refs: The Miercurea-Ciuc internment camp records, 1938

stops.name: Moroeni, the clinic and the release
stops.date_confidence: Attested: illness in October 1938, transfer to a clinic at Moroeni, release on 12 November 1938, per the English Wikipedia article, corroborated on the release date by the New World Encyclopedia. That article describes the release as unconditional, 'simply released on November 12', rather than granted on medical grounds. The coordinate is Nominatim's for Moroeni in Dambovita, correcting a working figure 12 kilometres north in the Bucegi foothills.
stops.campa: A sanatorium in the Dambovita foothills, pines, a rest cure for a tubercular lung, and on the twelfth of November they let him go. The order carries no condition attached to it and no stated reason. He is thirty-one, and has been in custody since the fourteenth of July. He goes back to Bucharest, to the apartment on Dacia Boulevard and to the lectures, expecting to take up an ordinary career there. Within eighteen months he is out of the country on a government passport, and he never lives in Romania again.
suggested_refs: The clinic at Moroeni, Dambovita, and the release order of 12 November 1938

stops.name: London, the Romanian Legation
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade became cultural press attache at the Romanian Legation in London in April 1940 and was transferred after Britain broke relations with Axis-aligned Romania in February 1941, per the English Wikipedia article; the day is a default. The legation address was not located in any source reached, so the pin is approximate central London.
stops.campa: The Foreign Ministry sends him to London as cultural press attache, which means placing articles about Romania in a country that is being bombed. He arrives in April 1940, and by September the Blitz is over his lodgings. Romania meanwhile falls into the German orbit, loses Bessarabia to the Soviets and northern Transylvania to Hungary, and in February 1941 Britain breaks off relations. The legation staff are put on a train. From here on, his war is spent in the one country in Europe where nothing happens.
suggested_refs: Romanian Legation correspondence, London, 1940-1941

stops.name: Hotel Palacio, Estoril
stops.date_confidence: Attested that on transfer to Portugal Eliade stayed at the Hotel Palacio in Estoril, per the English Wikipedia article; the day is a default and the month follows the February 1941 transfer date given there.
stops.campa: The Hotel Palacio at Estoril in 1941 holds the whole wartime traffic of neutral Europe in one lobby: deposed kings on allowances, refugees waiting on American visas, German and British agents at adjacent tables under an understanding that nobody shoots inside the Casino. Eliade takes a room here as the press officer of a country that has just joined the Axis. He walks down to the sea, writes in Romanian, and reads the wire copy from the eastern front for news of a war his own government has entered against Russia.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Palacio, Estoril, and the wartime diplomatic colony on the Portuguese Riviera

stops.name: Romanian Legation, Lisbon: the book on Salazar
stops.date_confidence: Attested: press officer and cultural attache at the Romanian Legation in Lisbon from February 1941, through the National Legionary State and then Antonescu's regime, publishing Salazar si revolutia in Portugalia in 1942 and Romanii, latinii Orientului in 1943, per the English Wikipedia article and the books' own publication. The precise legation address was not located; the pin is central Lisbon. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: His task in Lisbon is to make Romania legible to Portuguese readers, and he performs it by writing a book about Salazar: a corporatist Catholic dictatorship run by an economics professor, presented as the model of a nation reorganized around its own spirit instead of around parties. It sells. He follows it with Romanii, latinii Orientului, arguing Romania into Latin Europe. In the same rooms, on the same government salary, he is drafting the comparative morphology of the sacred that will make his name in Paris.
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Salazar si revolutia in Portugalia (Bucharest, 1942)
Mircea Eliade, Romanii, latinii Orientului (Lisbon, 1943)

stops.name: Cascais, the Portuguese journal
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade found a house in Cascais on Rua da Saudade, per the English Wikipedia article. The coordinate is flagged rather than asserted: Nominatim finds no Rua da Saudade in Cascais town, only three in the wider municipality between five and nine kilometres east, so the pin is Cascais town centre and the house is not located. The date orders the segment. The Carl Schmitt remark is attested through the corpus file rene_guenon.journey.json, which quotes the Portugal Journal.
stops.campa: The house at Cascais is where the Portuguese journal is kept, and the journal is the one document of these years he wrote for nobody. In it he hopes for a German victory over the Soviet Union, then reads Stalingrad and stops hoping; he records insomnia, self-disgust, Nina coughing in the next room, and Carl Schmitt's remark to him that Rene Guenon is the most interesting person of the age. The journal appears in Romanian in 2006 and in English, in Mac Linscott Ricketts's translation, in 2010.
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, The Portugal Journal, trans. Mac Linscott Ricketts (2010)

stops.name: Lisbon, the death of Nina Mares
stops.date_confidence: The marriage year and the month of death are attested: Romanian Wikipedia gives 'Nina (n. Mares, d. noiembrie 1944), cu care s-a casatorit in 1934'. The exact day, 20 November, is carried from the dossier and was not confirmed by any source re-fetched this pass; the sources reached give only November 1944. An attempted fetch of a dedicated page on Nina Mares returned 404.
stops.campa: Uterine cancer, found too late, treated in a foreign country on a legation salary through the last winter of the war. Nina dies in Lisbon in November 1944, and Eliade writes in the journal that he has considered killing himself. He does not. He goes back to the manuscript instead, working in the room where she died, and out of that winter comes the book Paris will publish in 1949 as the Traite d'histoire des religions. Her daughter Giza stays with him.
suggested_refs: The Portugal Journal entries for November 1944

stops.name: Paris, arrival on 16 September 1945
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the English Wikipedia article dates the move to France to 16 September 1945 and records that Eliade travelled with his adopted daughter Giza. The pin is the canonical corpus coordinate for Paris.
stops.campa: Romania is occupied by the Red Army and is being converted into a people's republic. A former Legionary publicist who spent the war as an Antonescu diplomat cannot go back, and does not try. He crosses into France on the sixteenth of September 1945 with Giza and no position: thirty-eight years old, holding a doctorate from a university now inside the Soviet bloc, and a bibliography written largely in a language nobody in Paris reads. He starts again in French, which he does not yet write well.
suggested_refs: The French residence permits issued to Romanian exiles, 1945-1946

stops.name: Ecole pratique des hautes etudes, Dumezil's chair
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Georges Dumezil arranged lectures for Eliade at the Ecole pratique des hautes etudes and wrote the preface to the 1949 Traite. The starting year is approximate and the day and month are defaults: the sources reached describe the Paris period as running 1945 to 1956 without dating the first course.
stops.campa: Georges Dumezil, who has spent twenty years demonstrating that the Indo-European peoples sorted their gods the way they sorted their societies, gets the Romanian a lectern. Around him at the Ecole: Henry Corbin on the Iranian angelology, Louis Massignon on al-Hallaj, Bataille, Ricoeur, Jean Danielou. Cioran and the rest of the Romanian exile are in the same city, arguing in cafes about what each of them had been in 1937. Eliade lives off the lectures, off translations and off articles for eleven years, and holds no professorship in France at all.
suggested_refs: Georges Dumezil's preface to the Traite d'histoire des religions (1949)

stops.name: Paris, the two books of 1949
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Techniques du Yoga in 1948 and, in 1949, both the Traite d'histoire des religions and Le Mythe de l'eternel retour, per the English Wikipedia article. The day and month are defaults; the pin repeats the Ecole pratique coordinate for want of a located writing address. The quotation is page-cited by a secondary source consulted directly and was not checked against the printed page.
stops.campa: Two books in one year lay down the whole apparatus. The Traite sorts the religions of the world not by people or period but by the form the sacred takes when it shows itself: sky, water, stone, tree, moon, the shapes that recur everywhere because human beings everywhere stand at the same distance from what they are not. Le Mythe de l'eternel retour then argues that archaic man refused history outright, abolishing profane time by repeating the acts of the gods. Dumezil writes the preface to the first of them.
stops.quote: The crude product of nature, the object fashioned by the industry of man, acquire their reality, their identity, only to the extent of their participation in a transcendent reality.
stops.quote_source: Mircea Eliade, Cosmos and History: The Myth of the Eternal Return, trans. Willard R. Trask, p. 5
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Traite d'histoire des religions (Payot, 1949)
Mircea Eliade, Le Mythe de l'eternel retour (Gallimard, 1949)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hierophany', citing the Trask translations with page numbers

stops.name: Paris, the marriage to Christinel Cotescu
stops.date_confidence: Attested and dated exactly by Romanian Wikipedia: 'a doua sotie a fost Christinel (n. Cotescu, d. 9 martie 1998), cu care s-a casatorit, la Paris, in 9 ianuarie 1950'. Some secondary summaries give 1948; the archival date resolves against them and the earlier hedge is dropped.
stops.campa: Christinel Cotescu, of the Romanian exile, sister-in-law of the conductor Ionel Perlea, marries him in Paris on the ninth of January 1950. She becomes his secretary, his copyist, his translator, the keeper of his appointments, and in the end the keeper of his papers. After 1986 she holds them for twelve years and decides what of them gets published. She dies on the ninth of March 1998, which is the date he insisted all his life was his birthday and which the Bucharest registry says was not.
suggested_refs: Christinel Eliade's stewardship of the Eliade papers, 1986-1998

stops.name: Casa Eranos, the first Tagung
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 'In 1950, Eliade began attending Eranos conferences' (English Wikipedia); the day is a default. The invitation from Olga Frobe-Kapteyn dated 5 October 1949, and Henry Corbin's role in recommending him, are dossier-only: eranosfoundation.org and eranos.org both returned 404 this pass and Nominatim holds no record for a Fondazione Eranos, so neither could be confirmed. The pin is the canonical corpus Eranos coordinate.
stops.campa: Olga Frobe-Kapteyn has been convening these August meetings on the lake below Monte Verita since 1933: a long table under the trees at Moscia where no discipline is permitted to dismiss another. Eliade comes for the first time in 1950 and finds Jung at the head of it, with Corbin, Scholem, Kerenyi, Portmann, and Giuseppe Tucci, whom he last saw in a Calcutta drawing room twenty-one years earlier. He speaks in French. He is printed in the yearbook, and he comes back nearly every year for the next decade and a half.
suggested_refs: The Eranos-Jahrbuch volumes carrying Eliade's Ascona lectures from 1950

stops.name: Eranos, Jung's last lecture
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to Eliade's presence. Jung's final Eranos lecture, on synchronicity, in August 1951 is attested in the corpus files jung.journey.json and olga_frobe_kapteyn.journey.json; no source names Eliade in that room. His attendance from 1950 onward is attested, so presence at the 1951 Tagung is inference and is recorded as such. The day is a default.
stops.campa: Jung, seventy-six, gives his last Eranos lecture, and it is on synchronicity: the claim that meaningful coincidence is a category of connection standing alongside cause. Eliade, in his second year at the table, is assembling an argument that runs beside it without ever touching it, that the sacred manifests itself in objects and that the manifestation is the foundation of a world rather than a projection onto one. Neither man adopts the other's vocabulary. They are courteous about each other in print for the rest of their lives.
suggested_refs: C. G. Jung, 'On Synchronicity', Eranos lecture, August 1951

stops.name: Eranos, the yearbook years
stops.date_confidence: Attested in general terms that Eliade returned to Eranos repeatedly through the 1960s. The roster is attested by olga_frobe_kapteyn.journey.json, which records that by 1961 she had convened twenty-nine August meetings and names Eliade among the speakers. No individual year after 1950 is separately confirmed here; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: By 1961 Frobe-Kapteyn has run twenty-nine of these August weeks and edited thirty volumes of the yearbook, and Eliade's name stands on that roster with Jung, Kerenyi, Corbin, Scholem, Suzuki, Martin Buber, and Wolfgang Pauli lecturing on Kepler above the lake. He already has an audience. What Ascona supplies is a room in which comparative religion, depth psychology, Islamic mysticism and quantum physics count as one conversation, which no university department in Europe will grant him. He keeps coming back.
suggested_refs: The Eranos-Jahrbuch series, 1933-1988, and the speaker roster through 1961

stops.name: Swift Hall, the Haskell Lectures
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 'In 1956, Eliade accepted an appointment as a Visiting Professor at the University of Chicago, where he delivered the Haskell Lectures on the history of religions' (University of Chicago Library, Guide to the Mircea Eliade Papers 1926-1998). Joachim Wach's role in issuing the invitation is dossier-only: Wach is not mentioned anywhere in that finding aid. The month is a default. The pin is the canonical corpus University of Chicago coordinate; Nominatim gives Swift Hall itself as 41.7889, -87.6001.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic at forty-nine to give a course of lectures in a neo-Gothic divinity school on the South Side of Chicago, and stays thirty years. The lectures become The Sacred and the Profane. Joachim Wach, the German exile who built the history of religions at Chicago and who is usually credited with bringing him over, dies before the appointment is settled, and the chair Eliade is offered is Wach's own. He takes it in a country whose language he learned in middle age.
suggested_refs: The Haskell Lectures on the history of religions, University of Chicago, autumn 1956
sources: University of Chicago Library, 'Guide to the Mircea Eliade Papers 1926-1998'

stops.name: Chicago, the permanent move
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade moved to the United States in 1957 and became professor in the Divinity School and a member of the Committee on Social Thought, per the New World Encyclopedia and the English Wikipedia article; the day and month are defaults. The quotation is verified verbatim inside the book by full-text search at Open Library, and carries no comma after 'sacred', against the punctuation given on some secondary pages.
stops.campa: He settles in Hyde Park with Christinel, in an apartment full of Romanian books, and begins the American thirty years. The Sacred and the Profane goes out to a general readership and states the position in one line near the top of the argument. Everything he writes afterward elaborates it: the sacred is not a feeling about the world but the thing that makes a world out of undifferentiated space, and a people without a center is a people that cannot say where it is standing.
stops.quote: The manifestation of the sacred ontologically founds the world.
stops.quote_source: Mircea Eliade, The Sacred and the Profane: The Nature of Religion, trans. Willard R. Trask, p. 21
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Das Heilige und das Profane (1957), translated as The Sacred and the Profane (1959)
sources: Open Library full-text search of the Trask translation

stops.name: Chicago, the founding of History of Religions
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the journal History of Religions was founded in 1961 by Eliade and published by the University of Chicago Press, per Wikipedia's article on the journal; the University of Chicago finding aid says he 'co-founded and edited' it. The named co-founders, Joseph Kitagawa and Charles Long, appear in neither source and are carried here as reconstruction. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: A journal is the instrument by which a subject becomes a discipline. It decides what counts as a contribution, who may referee, and which questions are live. Eliade founds History of Religions in 1961 and edits it, and inside a decade the Chicago school is what a doctorate in the field means in the United States. Joseph Kitagawa and Charles Long are named beside him as co-founders in most accounts of it. The two sources reachable here name only Eliade.
suggested_refs: History of Religions, University of Chicago Press, volume 1 (1961)
sources: University of Chicago Library, 'Guide to the Mircea Eliade Papers 1926-1998'

stops.name: Chicago, the Avery chair
stops.date_confidence: Attested: named Sewell L. Avery Distinguished Service Professor in 1964, per the English Wikipedia article and the New World Encyclopedia; the day and month are defaults. Election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1966 is dossier-derived and was not independently confirmed this pass. The Frye quotation reaches here through a Contemporary Authors entry reproduced at Encyclopedia.com, which does not give Frye's original venue.
stops.campa: The university makes him Sewell L. Avery Distinguished Service Professor at fifty-seven. Northrop Frye says the impressive thing about the work is not the erudition but the single pattern running under yoga, literature, archaic ritual and alchemy; the critics who distrust the pattern describe it in almost the same words and mean it as the charge. Myth and Reality comes out in 1963, the English Shamanism in 1964, and he is by now the man Americans read when they want to be told what religion is.
stops.quote: the most impressive thing about Eliade's works was not the breadth of his erudition, but the unity and the consistency with which he brought together yoga, literature, primitive religions, and alchemy to form a pattern
stops.quote_source: Northrop Frye, quoted in the Contemporary Authors entry for Mircea Eliade reproduced at Encyclopedia.com
suggested_refs: Mircea Eliade, Myth and Reality (1963)
Mircea Eliade, Shamanism: Archaic Techniques of Ecstasy (1964)

stops.name: Chicago, Maitreyi Devi comes to the office
stops.date_confidence: The encounter is attested: Wikipedia's article on Maitreyi Devi records that she travelled to the University of Chicago to lecture, where Eliade was a professor, and met with him several times. The year 1973 is dossier-derived and appears in no source reached this pass. Na Hanyate was published in 1974 and took the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1976. The day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: Forty-three years after Bhowanipore, Maitreyi Devi comes to Chicago on a lecture tour and asks to see him. She has learned, from a visiting Romanian, what is in the novel he published under her name in 1933 and never mentioned to her. They meet several times in his office. She goes home and writes Na Hanyate, It Does Not Die, which contradicts his account line by line and is itself a novel. It appears in 1974 and takes the Sahitya Akademi Award two years after that.
suggested_refs: Maitreyi Devi, Na Hanyate (1974), translated as It Does Not Die (1976)

stops.name: Meadville Lombard, the fire in the office
stops.date_confidence: Sources conflict on the year and the conflict is left open. The English Wikipedia article places the fire four months before Eliade's death, which is December 1985; the University of Chicago Library finding aid dates it twice to 1986, 'shortly before Eliade's death in 1986' and 'letters damaged by a 1986 fire in Eliade's office'. The finding aid supplies the measurable consequence: roughly a fifth of the correspondence destroyed, the damaged remnant surviving as an unidentifiable subseries. The day is a default. The address of Meadville Lombard in 1985 is approximated from its historic Woodlawn Avenue campus.
stops.campa: Fire takes part of his office at Meadville Lombard, and with it letters: about a fifth of the correspondence of a man who corresponded with everybody, burned past the point where an archivist can tell one hand from another. What is left of it sits in the collection as a subseries nobody can identify. Eliade reads the fire as an omen, which is the reading his own method licenses and which nothing in the event requires. Four months later he is dead.
suggested_refs: Subseries 5 of the Mircea Eliade Papers, 'letters damaged by a 1986 fire in Eliade's office'
sources: University of Chicago Library, 'Guide to the Mircea Eliade Papers 1926-1998'

stops.name: Bernard Mitchell Hospital, the last eight days
stops.date_confidence: The death is attested: 22 April 1986 in Chicago, aged 79, per the English Wikipedia article and the New World Encyclopedia, which gives stroke complications as the cause. The circumstances of the stroke on 14 April, that he was reading Cioran's Exercices d'admiration and lost the power of speech, are dossier-derived from an account attributed to Christinel Eliade and could not be independently confirmed this pass.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of April he has a stroke while reading Cioran, who has been at the edge of his life since the Criterion platform in Bucharest fifty-three years earlier, and loses the power of speech. He is taken to the Bernard Mitchell Hospital and does not get it back. He dies on the twenty-second, aged seventy-nine, in the third country to give him a passport. The Encyclopedia of Religion, sixteen volumes he commissioned and organized and will be listed as editor in chief of, is a year from publication.
suggested_refs: The Encyclopedia of Religion, 16 vols. (Macmillan, 1987), edited in chief by Mircea Eliade

stops.name: Rockefeller Memorial Chapel, Bellow reads the golden room
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the memorial was held at Rockefeller Memorial Chapel before about 1,200 people and that Saul Bellow read Eliade's own account of the childhood golden room, per the English Wikipedia article. No date for the service appears in any source reached, so the date here orders the segment only. Cremation the day after the death is attested by Romanian Wikipedia: 'fiind incinerat a doua zi'.
stops.campa: Twelve hundred people in a neo-Gothic chapel on a Chicago campus, and Saul Bellow, his colleague on the Committee on Social Thought, stands up and reads Eliade's own account of the drawing room in Bucharest filled with a gold he could taste. The passage comes from the first volume of the autobiography, set down half a century after the minute it describes. The body had been cremated the day after the death. There is no Orthodox burial, no Romanian ground, no return of any kind. No source reached gives the date of the service.
suggested_refs: Rockefeller Memorial Chapel, 5850 South Woodlawn Avenue, Chicago

stops.name: Oak Woods Cemetery, the ashes
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Eliade's ashes are at Oak Woods Cemetery on Chicago's South Side, which lists him among its notable burials as 'Romanian historian of religion, fiction writer, philosopher, and professor at the University of Chicago'. No headstone text could be confirmed and no interment date appears in any source reached; the date orders the segment. The coordinate is Nominatim's for 1035 East 67th Street.
stops.campa: The ashes go into a South Side cemetery among Chicago mayors, Confederate prisoner dead and Olympic sprinters, under a stone identifying him as a historian of religion, a novelist and a professor at the university. Bryan Rennie records that the death was received as nothing less than a mahaparinirvana, the Buddhist term for the final passing of one who will not be reborn. The documentary record holds a stroke and eight days in a hospital. The term is often credited to Ioan Petru Culianu; no text reached this pass carries it in his hand.
stops.quote_source: Bryan S. Rennie, The International Eliade, characterizing how Eliade's death was received; the term is often attributed to Ioan Petru Culianu, an attribution that could not be traced to any text reached this pass
suggested_refs: Oak Woods Cemetery, 1035 East 67th Street, Chicago, notable burials list
sources: Bryan S. Rennie, The International Eliade, via Open Library full-text search

stops.name: 1100 East 57th Street, the Eliade Papers
stops.date_confidence: Attested in full by the University of Chicago Library finding aid: 'Guide to the Mircea Eliade Papers 1926-1998', 180 boxes and 90.75 linear feet at the Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center, 1100 East 57th Street, concentrated in the Chicago years 1957-1986 with material from the 1928-1930 India period and the 1945-1957 Paris years. The date is arbitrary and orders the segment; the collection accrued over years and its span runs to 1998. Culianu's murder on 21 May 1991 is attested by the English Wikipedia article on him.
stops.campa: One hundred and eighty boxes, ninety linear feet: manuscripts, typescripts, family photographs out of Romania, the India notebooks, the Paris correspondence, recordings of his voice, and the burned fifth nobody can read. In 1991 his student and designated heir Ioan Petru Culianu, who had begun writing publicly about the Legionary years, is shot dead in a washroom at the Divinity School a few blocks south of this reading room. The case has never been solved.
suggested_refs: Hanna Holborn Gray Special Collections Research Center, Mircea Eliade Papers 1926-1998
Ted Anton, Eros, Magic, and the Murder of Professor Culianu (1996)
sources: University of Chicago Library, 'Guide to the Mircea Eliade Papers 1926-1998'

stops.name: Bucharest, elected to the Academy after death
stops.date_confidence: Attested: posthumous election to the Romanian Academy in 1990, per the English Wikipedia article and the New World Encyclopedia; the day and month are defaults. The street and school namings and the Moldovan stamp are attested by Romanian Wikipedia, which gives no issue year for the stamp. Whether his work was formally banned under Ceausescu or merely left unprinted could not be settled by any source reached and is recorded as a gap.
stops.campa: Four years after his death and one year after the Ceausescu government falls, the Romanian Academy elects him. The country starts printing him again, and prints everything at once: the novels, the journals, the Romanian articles of the 1930s, the pieces about the Christian revolution included. Streets and schools take his name, a Bucharest boulevard takes his name, and the Republic of Moldova puts his face on a stamp. Whether the books had been banned outright or only left unprinted is not settled by anything reachable.
suggested_refs: The Romanian Academy's posthumous election of 1990
Micaela Ghitescu, 'Un centenar si o aniversare', Romania Literara, 13 April 2007

stops.name: Mantuleasa church, the bust before the school
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Romanian Wikipedia: a bust by the sculptor Vasile Gorduz unveiled on 28 March 2009 in front of the Mantuleasa church. The second bust, by Gheorghe Tanase, is attested there verbatim for 24 November 2015 at the corner of Bulevardul Mircea Eliade and Strada Aviator Radu Beller, opposite Parcul Floreasca, which Nominatim places at 44.4645, 26.0957.
stops.campa: Vasile Gorduz's bronze head goes up in front of the Mantuleasa church, a short walk from the primary school, in the street he had turned into a novella about an old man whose stories the secret police cannot reach the end of. It is unveiled on the twenty-eighth of March 2009. Six years later a second bust, by Gheorghe Tanase, is set at the corner of the boulevard that carries his name, opposite Parcul Floreasca. The first stands at number 20, facing the church door.
